lesson.title: What Everything Is Made Of: An Introduction to Matter
lesson.summary: This section introduces matter as anything with mass that occupies space, and shows how its three common states differ at the particle level.
lesson.body:
Every object you can touch, every breath of air you take, and every drop of water you drink has something in common: all of it is matter. Chemists define matter simply as anything that has mass and occupies space, meaning it takes up a measurable volume. This definition might seem obvious for a rock or a glass of water, but it also includes things you cannot see or feel easily, like the air filling a balloon. The air has mass, you could weigh a filled balloon and an empty one and find a real difference, and it occupies the balloon's interior volume, so it counts as matter even though it is invisible. Light, heat, and sound are not matter. They are forms of energy that can move through matter or empty space, but they have no mass of their own and occupy no fixed volume.

Matter commonly exists in three familiar states: solid, liquid, and gas, and a fourth state called plasma exists at very high temperatures, such as inside stars or fluorescent lights. What distinguishes these states is not what the matter is made of, but how its particles are arranged and how much energy they have. In a solid, particles are packed tightly in fixed positions, vibrating in place but not moving past one another, which is why solids hold a definite shape and volume. In a liquid, particles are still close together but have enough energy to slide past each other, so a liquid takes the shape of its container while keeping a fixed volume. In a gas, particles are far apart and move independently at high speed, spreading out to fill whatever container holds them, so gases have neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume.

Water offers a clean example of how one substance can exist in all three familiar states without changing what it fundamentally is. Ice, liquid water, and water vapor are all made of the same particles, H2O molecules, arranged and moving differently depending on temperature. Below 0 degrees Celsius at normal atmospheric pressure, those molecules lock into the rigid lattice of ice. Between 0 and 100 degrees Celsius, they have enough energy to flow past each other as liquid water. Above 100 degrees Celsius, they gain enough energy to break free of each other entirely and spread out as steam. The chemical identity never changes, only the physical arrangement of the same H2O molecules.

It is also worth separating two ideas that get confused in everyday speech: mass and weight. Mass measures the actual amount of matter in an object, and it does not change no matter where the object is located. Weight measures the force of gravity pulling on that mass, and it does change with location. An astronaut with a mass of 70 kilograms has that same mass on Earth, on the Moon, or drifting in space, but her weight on the Moon is only about one sixth of her weight on Earth, because the Moon's gravitational pull is weaker. Chemists almost always care about mass rather than weight, since mass reflects the actual quantity of matter being studied.

Recognizing something as matter is only the first step. Chemistry is largely the science of classifying matter and explaining why different kinds of matter behave differently, and that classification system is built in layers. The next sections in this unit will start from the smallest scale, the atom, and build upward through elements, compounds, and mixtures, giving you a structured way to describe any sample of matter you encounter, from a pure gold ring to a glass of salt water.
